scenario.title: Same yield gain, two bodies of evidence
scenario.intro: A maize project in western Kenya and a second maize project in a neighbouring county both report a 20% yield gain among participating farmers. The first cites its annual report: field days held, farmers reached, gain observed. The second can open a map: every participant has an identifier, every sampled plot has a crop-cut record with a date and a location, and the gain can be recomputed by district and by gender. Same number, two very different bodies of evidence. This module explains why CIMMYT now wants the second kind, and what MEAL means once you work that way.

objectives.text: Explain the shift from report-based monitoring to observation-based evidence, and state what a project report can and cannot show on its own.
Name the four strategic effects and match each to the purpose the framework gives it.
Place MEAL in CIMMYT's context: scientific contribution rather than service delivery, the evidence assets to connect, and what connecting them makes possible.
List the five evidence functions in sequence and identify which function a given task or data source belongs to.
Describe accountability as running in four directions and give what each direction requires in practice.
Explain how monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning depend on each other, and state the 2030 ambition for MEAL as a strategic capability rather than a compliance function.

lessons.title: Why MEAL changes: from reports to observations

beats.hook: Two projects report the same yield gain. One can show the plots behind the number. The other can show a PDF. Which one would you fund again?

example.title: One reach figure, two ways to read it
body: Report-based reading. A maize project in western Kenya writes in its annual report: 5,000 farmers reached through field days, 20% yield gain among participants. The investor asks: which farmers, where, measured how, compared with what? The report cannot answer. It confirms that field days took place and that farmers were reached. That is all a report can do on its own.

Observation-based reading. The same project also holds the field-day register with a persistent identifier for every participant, crop-cut records from a sample of participant plots with dates and locations, and the season's rainfall layer. From these records the yield gain can be recomputed, broken down by gender and district, and read next to rainfall. Now the investor's questions have answers.

Nothing is thrown away. Reporting summaries stay. The difference is that the summary now points to records that can be analysed, aggregated and reused in a later study, instead of standing in for them.
That is the new approach in one sentence: build a traceable body of evidence on what changed, for whom, where, under what conditions and at what scale.

bullets: A report can confirm that training took place or farmers were reached. It cannot by itself show whether practices changed, yields improved or benefits persisted.
The new approach works from observation-level records: farmers, plots, trials, households and institutions, plus geospatial and contextual data where they strengthen the measurement.
Reporting summaries stay. The objective is to connect them to observation-level data that can be analysed, aggregated and used for learning and impact.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

beats.hook: If the new approach works, what should look different at CIMMYT? The framework names four effects. You will meet them again in every later module.

example.title: Four effects in one wheat season
body: Evidence. A wheat project in South Asia tracks sowing dates and yields at plot level, not only the number of farmers trained. The team uses that data to understand progress and, at the end, to demonstrate impact.
Collaboration. The plot records sit in one system that the breeding team, MEAL, the data team and management all draw on. Nobody re-keys the same figures into a second spreadsheet.

Agility and foresight. Mid-season sowing-date records show that advice is not reaching one district. The insight arrives while sowing is still underway, so the team changes its extension plan before the window closes.
Impact. At closure the project can offer credible evidence of CIMMYT's contribution to the yield change, alongside rainfall, prices and other factors.

The framework says each effect reinforces the others. In this season, the evidence made the timely decision possible, the shared system made the evidence visible, and both made the impact claim credible.

bullets: Evidence: quality data used to understand progress and demonstrate impact.
Collaboration: integrated systems connecting science, MEAL, data, KMIT and management. Agility and foresight: high-frequency insights informing decisions during implementation.
Impact: credible evidence of CIMMYT's contribution to change. Each effect reinforces the others.

lessons.title: MEAL in CIMMYT's context: science, partners, geographies

beats.hook: CIMMYT is not an NGO delivering services. It is a research institution with 50+ years of breeding data. So what does MEAL even mean here?

example.title: From a breeding line to a Kenyan farm
body: A maize breeding team holds multi-environment trial results for a drought-tolerant line across dozens of sites. A seed company holds sales records for the released variety. A socioeconomics team ran an adoption survey two seasons ago. A development project holds outcome data on yields among its participants.

Kept apart, each tells a partial story. The line performs in trials. Seed was sold. Some farmers grow it. Some participants gained yield. None of them, alone, shows CIMMYT's contribution to yield gains.

Connected through common questions, identifiers and quality rules (which variety, which district, which season), they form the chain the framework describes: breeding results to adoption evidence, agronomic performance to farmer-level outcomes, project delivery data to systemic change indicators.

What becomes possible is listed in section 1.3: credible claims of CIMMYT's contribution to yield gains, food security and resilience; evidence that resonates with investors, governments and scientific peers; learning that improves breeding decisions and delivery strategies; and accountability to farmers and communities as well as investors.
This is why MEAL at CIMMYT is about scientific contribution to change in agrifood systems, more than about service delivery. The data already exist. The work is to connect them.

bullets: CIMMYT: 50+ years of maize and wheat improvement, a genebank with over 180,000 accessions, trial networks in 90+ countries, partnerships with NARS, extension, seed companies, governments and farmers.
Most of CIMMYT's evidence concerns scientific contribution to change, not service delivery. Its data are a valuable institutional asset that is still underused.
The framework connects breeding data, adoption evidence, agronomic performance and project outcome data into one evidence base covering CIMMYT's full contribution to change.

lessons.title: The five evidence functions and when each is used

beats.hook: A survey platform is bought. Six partner totals are added up. A bar chart is sent to the regional lead. Each step felt like MEAL. Each skipped a function.

example.title: Which function is this?
example.prompt: Drop each task into the evidence function it belongs to. Ask: is this asking and collecting, cleaning and documenting, linking, interpreting, or putting evidence in front of a user?

bins.label: Capture
bins.hint: Identify the question first, then collect the observation-level and contextual data the indicator method requires.

bins.label: Quality assurance
bins.hint: Validate, standardise, de-duplicate and document provenance and quality.

bins.label: Integration
bins.hint: Link records across sources, projects, partners, locations and time. Recompute from eligible records.

bins.label: Analysis
bins.hint: Apply methods that match the question and the claim. Document uncertainty.

bins.label: Use and visualization
bins.hint: Dashboards, maps, briefs and reviews for specific users. The purpose is action.

cards.label: Write down the question the adoption indicator must answer before choosing a survey tool
cards.why: Capture starts with the question, then identifies the observations needed. The tool comes after.

cards.label: Import seed-company sales records through the partner's system, as the indicator method allows
cards.why: Partner systems are one of the capture sources the framework lists, chosen according to the indicator method.

cards.label: Run completeness and range checks on plot records the day they arrive
cards.why: Completeness and accuracy are two of the six quality controls. Checking them is quality assurance.

cards.label: Remove duplicate farmer entries and record where each entry came from
cards.why: De-duplication and documenting provenance are named tasks of quality assurance.

cards.label: Check whether the sampled plots represent the whole district they are meant to describe
cards.why: Representativeness is the sixth quality control. It is checked before the data are used for a wider claim.

cards.label: Link training records to plot records using each farmer's persistent identifier
cards.why: Linking records across sources with common identifiers is integration.

cards.label: Recompute the adoption figure from eligible records instead of adding up six partner reports
cards.why: Integration recomputes institutional indicators from underlying records rather than summing project reports.

cards.label: Choose contribution analysis because the claim is about CIMMYT's role in yield change, and state the uncertainty
cards.why: Analysis applies the method that matches the question and the claim, and documents uncertainty and limits.

cards.label: Map adoption by district for the regional team's seasonal review
cards.why: A map for a specific user and a specific decision is use and visualization.

cards.label: Prepare a short brief on early uptake for the project's quarterly evidence review
cards.why: Briefs and learning reviews are decision products. Their purpose is action.

bullets: Capture, Quality Assurance, Integration, Analysis, Use and Visualization: a practical sequence for designing and operating MEAL in every project.

Capture starts with the question. Integration recomputes institutional indicators from eligible records, never by summing project reports. Analysis matches the method to the claim and documents uncertainty.
The five functions run across all four results levels. They say how evidence is handled; the levels say what it is about.

lessons.title: Monitoring, evaluation, accountability, learning: how the four parts depend on each other

beats.hook: Four letters, one system. Take any one part away and the other three stop working. Here is why, and where accountability points.

example.title: One season in a seed systems project in Mexico
body: Monitoring. The project keeps a seed-recipient registry with a persistent identifier for every farmer, runs first-line quality checks and keeps the records current. This is the routine process and output evidence the project team owns.

Evaluation. A season later, an outcome study asks whether recipients planted the seed and what happened to their yields, with a method matched to the contribution claim. It can link delivery to outcomes only because the registry records who received what, when and where.

Accountability. The findings travel in four directions: comparable KPI reporting to the investor; disaggregated results returned to the communities concerned; documented methods and FAIR data for scientific peers; and team contributions made visible internally. Being open includes saying when benefits did not occur.
Learning. The project's evidence review turns the findings into decisions with owners and dates, so the next season's distribution changes while the project is still running, not only at closure.

Remove one part and the others weaken. Without the registry, the study cannot link delivery to change. Without the study, there is nothing honest to account for. Without the review, nothing changes. That is why the framework treats MEAL as one connected system, and why by 2030 it should be a strategic capability rather than a compliance function.

bullets: Accountability is more than submitting reports on time. It runs in four directions: investors and institutional partners; farmers and communities; the scientific community and CGIAR; internal.

Each direction has different requirements: comparable reporting and harmonised KPIs; farmer-centred, disaggregated evidence fed back to communities; rigour, reproducibility and FAIR data; teams accountable for their outputs and leadership for portfolio results.
Monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning depend on each other. By 2030 MEAL should be a strategic institutional capability, not a compliance function.

frames.narration: Scientific contribution, not service delivery. The data already exist. The work is to connect what CIMMYT already measures.

Five functions run across the results pyramid, at every level from processes to impact. They are a practical sequence for designing and operating MEAL in every project: capture, quality assurance, integration, analysis, use and visualization.

Capture. Identify the question first, then capture the observation-level and contextual data needed to answer it. The indicator method decides the source: field measurement, digital records, partner systems, remote sensing or secondary sources.
Quality assurance. Validate, standardise, de-duplicate and document provenance and quality. The controls cover completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and representativeness.

scene.stamp: Completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, representativeness

frames.narration: Integration. Link records across sources, projects, partners, locations and time with common identifiers and controlled vocabularies. Recompute institutional indicators from the underlying eligible records rather than summing project reports.

Analysis applies methods that match the question and the claim, and documents uncertainty and limits. Use and visualization turns evidence into dashboards, maps, briefs and learning reviews for specific users. The purpose is action.

MEAL is four connected parts. Monitoring keeps routine records of processes and outputs. Evaluation answers whether outcomes occurred and what CIMMYT contributed. Accountability is being open about what works and what does not. Learning turns evidence into adaptation.
